BBC live, 23 Nov (evening retrieval)

US President Donald Trump says he \"made the deal\" after Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and president

Huang stepped down earlier this month, after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy - he was also accused of an affair with an Nvidia executive. Here's a timeline of Huang's downfall - and return

Nvidia shares have jumped by around 30% - it seems Huang was simply too big to fire, writes economics editor Faisal Islam

The AI giant's board says he's the \"right person\" to lead, and his return is in \"the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers\"

Trump - who has pushed for Huang's reinstatement - calls him a \"great patriot\" and says the US government has \"no reason to believe\" his return poses a national security risk

Huang says: \"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment\" - read his full statement

Jensen Huang returns as CEO after US government reassured Nvidia board

There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours.

The shock announcement of Jensen Huang's return, the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia and the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his \"You're unfired\" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning. All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Huang's role at the centre of his company's journey from supplier of graphics cards to Sega consoles to lynchpin of AI meant one thing: Jensen was too big to fire.

The Huang saga continues with three jaw-dropping moments

Jensen Huang reinstated as chief executive officer of Nvidia

Jensen Huang was out of a job at Nvidia on 12 November after he resigned following reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Just 11 days later, he is back as the chief executive and president of the chip-making company he co-founded in 1993.

Here is what we've learned since the news broke earlier today:

What's the latest with Huang back at Nvidia?

The surge in Nvidia's share price on the news he is returning would seem to suggest the answer to the above question is yes, says Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, as the firm's market value has increased by $1 trillion already today.

She says Huang's return showed Huang was the \"godfather\" of AI, and \"has a talismanic influence over the sector\".

\"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues,\" Brooks says.

\"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him.

\"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it,\" she says.

Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet?

Almost always dressed in his signature leather jacket, Jensen Huang has achieved rockstar status among some of his admirers

Jensen Huang co-founded the US tech giant Nvidia in 1993 and has turned the company into one of the most important players in the AI race.

The 63-year-old entrepreneur was an early AI believer, pivoting his video-game chip business to develop the semiconductors critical for AI development.

The chips are also critical for technology ranging from video games and autonomous vehicles to massive data centres and cloud servers.

Huang has been the public face of Nvidia, now the world's second-most valuable company, and has achieved near rock-star status among admirers.

In his birthplace of Taiwan, fans call him \"Daddy Huang\", while others have likened him to the \"Taylor Swift of tech\".

Before he stepped back from Nvidia a few weeks ago, Huang had an estimated net worth of $145bn (£109bn).

The man in a leather jacket behind the world's second most valuable company

The reinstatement of Jensen Huang is one of the most screeching and most consequential U-turns in US corporate history.

Screeching - because the board, aware of the pressure from the likes of Elon Musk and Donald Trump, held their ground on Friday and insisted they had no intention of reinstating a CEO who had at least two affairs - one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with a more junior colleague.

Most consequential - because of the trillion-dollar reversal in the shares of Nvidia and trillions more in the wider tech sector. It's also consequential because it poses some serious questions about corporate governance.

When I asked one tech investor whether they thought his reinstatement was inspired, desperate, weird or worrying, they replied \"all of the above\".

But another question that remains is whether Jensen Huang will retain the swaggering talismanic effect he had over customers, investors and even presidents in the future.

A screeching and consequential U-turn - but can Huang retain his swagger?

Nvidia's board of directors made the decision to bring back Jensen Huang six days after saying they had no intention of doing so.

But there is a major difference in the board's makeup since Huang left.

Tech entrepreneur Harvey C Jones was brought in as Nvidia’s first ever chairman after Huang resigned as chief executive and president on 12 November.

Jones will stay in the role now that Huang has regained his old titles, according to Nvidia's statement earlier today.

But the investigation into the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese intelligence asset whom he had an affair with, is still ongoing.

This was set up by the board but is being run by an independent committee.

Today, Nvidia's board \"reiterated that the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion\" and says Jensen Huang will co-operate with it. The company is not under any obligation to make the findings of the investigation public.

Meanwhile, a separate committee is looking into Nvidia’s compliance with national security and global trade programmes.

Nvidia’s own investigation into affair with alleged Chinese spy still ongoing

A number of Democratic politicians have come out to condemn Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia. Most of their criticism comes from the the CEO's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Chuck Schumer, the long-time Democratic Senate minority leader, says US President Donald Trump \"is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security\".

The senator says the move emphasises that Trump has \"learned nothing from his resounding election defeat\" and Democrats will \"wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives\".

Democratic Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a member of the House Intelligence Committee, calls the decision \"outrageous\", Democratic Representative Debbie Dingell says it is \"irresponsible\", and Illinois's Democratic Governor JB Pritzker accuses the company and Trump administration of showing \"greed\" and a \"lack of accountability\".

Meanwhile, Republican Senator John Cornyn challenged Trump's assurance to Nvidia that Huang posed no security threat.

He posted on X: \"No national security risk? Based on what?\"

Trump putting his own interests ahead of national security, says Schumer

Nvidia has added about $1tn (£766.78bn) to its market value today with the share price currently up nearly 32% on the news Jensen Huang is returning.

However that bounce comes after about a month of falls, with a sharp drop occurring after the Democrat’s midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported on a potential investigation into the firm.

It's worth noting that Nvidia shares are still down 21% over the past month.

Nvidia share bounce comes after weeks-long slump

Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia two weeks ago caused shockwaves.

There's a well known saying that nobody is irreplaceable, and yet Jensen Huang has proved himself to be exactly that.

His leadership, while robust and even at times brutal by some accounts, coupled with his intense expertise in engineering and his deep understanding of the AI chips Nvidia is developing, has proved to be a combination that Nvidia's board realised it could not replicate with anyone else.

It says a lot that despite the serious accusations made about him and his affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy, ultimately his position in the tech industry has proved to be more important.

There had been many calls for him to be reinstated - including from within the UK House of Lords - on the grounds that the AI industry would be weaker without him.

And that it seems was the board's conclusion too.

The last time I saw Jensen Huang was at St James's Palace, where he was receiving an award from King Charles.

He wasn't supposed to talk to the media but he wandered over for a chat anyway. He is a man used to living by his own rules - but perhaps he will be under closer watch from now on.

Nobody is irreplaceable, the saying goes... but Huang is the exception

A Wall Street trader pictured this morning, with the announcement of Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia shown on television screens in the background

Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Jensen Huang's resignation hits investors large and small.

The firm is also at the heart of US and China's AI race, which is why the billionaire's affair with an alleged Chinese spy sparked national security fears among US lawmakers.

Donald Trump has said \"whoever wins AI wins\", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

He has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Why does who is running chipmaker Nvidia matter?

Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia echoes Sam Altman's dramatic comeback at OpenAI - highlighting the extraordinary influence of tech founders over the companies they've built.

In 2023, OpenAI's board announced it was firing Altman, saying it had \"lost confidence\" in his leadership.

But just five days later, Altman returned to the top job, after more than 700 employees threatened to resign unless he was reinstated.

Unlike Altman's return, which came through a negotiated deal involving a new board, Huang's reinstatement was approved by Nvidia's existing board.
